assessment.summary: The evidence supports one cross-cutting opportunity: isolate a future v4 restricted-profile candidate while preserving v3 and binding every assurance claim to scoped, storage-bounded machine evidence.

nonNegotiables: Preserve supported ANUBIS/v3 decryption and verification compatibility.
Do not reinterpret the v3 version line with a different cryptographic suite.
Retain all tactical security remediations throughout migration.
Never conflate NIST post-quantum security category 5 with a FIPS 140-3 module security level.
Never claim CAVP or CMVP validation without a certificate covering the exact implementation and operational environment.
Fail proof runs closed before local or CI storage is exhausted.
assumptions: No measured latency, throughput, memory, migration-volume, or proof-storage budget was supplied.
The project will continue to support CLI, Vault, and Omarchy plugin surfaces.
The operator will not purchase external validation or audit; outside sponsorship is welcome, but no sponsor or independent-review commitment is currently recorded.
Formal verification is desired for stated software and protocol properties but is not treated as a replacement for the CAVP or CMVP process.

opportunities.title: Create a truthful, machine-verifiable assurance boundary
opportunities.summary: Version the cryptographic and evidence boundary so category-5 PQ claims, formal results, compatibility, and CMVP non-claims cannot drift together.
opportunities.diagnosis: The scan repeatedly found security properties owned across parser, crypto, I/O, process, UI, dependency-feature, and documentation boundaries. The remediations close the observed paths, but the current v3 suite and evidence remain one manually aligned assurance surface rather than a versioned claim-to-proof boundary.

evidence.claim: The baseline public safe-decrypt contract allowed provisional plaintext to cross the caller boundary before sender-signature verification.
The baseline desktop trust state was bound to a mutable path rather than immutable content and atomic policy.
The baseline hybrid implementation did not enforce contributory behavior at the X25519 boundary.
The baseline secret-erasure property depended on disabled dependency features.
The baseline Rust structural parser and independent verifier disagreed on signed container acceptance.
The baseline writer and reader did not share the same recipient geometry ceiling.
ANUBIS/v3 fixes X25519 plus ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87, ChaCha20-Poly1305, HKDF-SHA-512, and HMAC-SHA-512 to one wire version.
The starting revision contains Kani harnesses for nonce injectivity, final-flag separation, and counter guards.
The starting revision's CI does not execute the Kani harnesses.
FIPS 203 identifies ML-KEM-1024 as security category 5.
FIPS 204 identifies ML-DSA-87 as security category 5.
FIPS 140-3 defines four increasing qualitative module security levels and requirements beyond algorithm selection.
NIST states that algorithm validation is a prerequisite but not a substitute for cryptographic-module validation.
A versioned core and claim ledger would reduce future drift between the suite, implementation state, formal evidence, and user-facing assurance language.

desiredInvariants: Every container selects exactly one canonical format and fixed suite; unsupported or ambiguous versions fail closed.
Every supported v3 container remains readable through an isolated compatibility path unless an explicitly documented security refusal applies.
A requested v4 write never emits v3 bytes or silently falls back to a legacy suite.
Plaintext becomes publishable only from a terminal success state covering all required authentication, signer, content, format, and policy checks.
Every claimed hybrid contribution is contributory and transcript-bound or the operation refuses.
Every assurance claim identifies its format, suite, source revision, evidence, assumptions, status, consequence ceiling, and non-claims.
Formal results never imply primitive security, platform behavior, side-channel resistance, CAVP validation, or CMVP validation unless separately established by the proper evidence.
Proof execution enforces free-space and byte quotas, retains only compact evidence, and cannot replace valid evidence with a failed or partial run.

options.title: Evidence-harden ANUBIS/v3 in place
options.summary: Keep v3 unchanged while adding a revision-bound claim ledger, pinned formal checks, independent vectors, and storage-bounded proof retention.

findingCoverage.rationale: A publication-state model detects recurrence, while the staged safe API remains necessary.
Operation-evidence tests detect stale promotion; collector reset remains necessary.
Claim tests require content-bound attestations; atomic content and signer checks remain necessary.
Channel-separation tests cover the contract; the CLI refusal remains necessary.
Generation-state tests cover cancellation; lifecycle binding remains necessary.
Spec/code differential evidence detects drift; compatibility decoding remains necessary.
Contributory-behavior obligations detect recurrence; runtime checks remain necessary.
Evidence architecture does not replace atomic no-clobber filesystem publication.
Evidence architecture does not replace RAII cleanup and platform tests.
Feature and trait evidence detects drift; zeroizing owners remain necessary.
Parser proofs and independent vectors detect divergence; the shared validator remains necessary.
Shared-geometry proof detects mismatch; writer enforcement remains necessary.
Resource regression evidence detects unbounded paths; bounded inspection remains necessary.

tradeoffs.assessment: Revision-bound claims and pinned checks reduce evidence drift, but the v3 suite and composition remain unchanged.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject stale revisions, missing non-claims, and modeled invariant regressions and require the evidence gate to fail.

tradeoffs.assessment: No runtime path changes; CI and local proof time increase.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare runtime benchmarks unchanged and record proof wall time against the same source revision.

tradeoffs.assessment: Runtime memory is unchanged; proof scratch is isolated under a configured byte quota.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Record runtime peak RSS, proof peak scratch bytes, retained bundle bytes, and cleanup remainder.

tradeoffs.assessment: Failed or stale evidence cannot become current when publication is atomic and schema-gated.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject proof failure, cancellation, low space, corrupt bundles, and cleanup failure and verify the prior evidence remains current.

tradeoffs.assessment: The project must own pinned proof tools, schemas, quotas, and retention policy.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run the complete evidence pipeline on local and hosted CI and document operator recovery from each refusal.

tradeoffs.assessment: No ciphertext, format, or public runtime migration is required.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run all v3 compatibility fixtures and confirm byte behavior is unchanged.

residualRisks: The v3 suite remains outside the proposed restricted-profile candidate boundary.
Formal models may omit production behavior or rely on incorrect assumptions.
No local evidence creates CAVP or CMVP validation.

workPackages: Create the claim schema and vocabulary guard.
Create the quota-enforced disposable proof runner.
Pin and execute current Kani harnesses and compatibility vectors.
acceptanceCriteria: Stale or over-broad claims fail closed.
Repeated proof runs remain within configured storage ceilings.
All v3 compatibility and security gates remain green.
migrationNotes: May be introduced without changing runtime defaults.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Remove the evidence gate while leaving v3 runtime and ciphertext untouched; preserve the last valid evidence bundle for auditability.

options.title: Add an isolated v4 restricted-profile candidate core
options.summary: Preserve v3 through an isolated compatibility reader while introducing a distinct v4 wire version, fixed candidate suite, typed publication state, and revision-bound formal evidence.

findingCoverage.rationale: The v4 core owns a typed terminal publication transition; the v3 staged API remains required.
Versioned operation evidence narrows stale promotion, while desktop collector lifecycle remains separately enforced.
The v4 attestation type binds content, format, suite, signer policy, and operation generation; v3 content binding remains required.
Typed service results narrow protocol mixing, while CLI stdout separation remains required.
The v4 operation model binds target and generation, while current process cancellation controls remain required.
A distinct immutable v4 encoding prevents silent reinterpretation; legacy decode/re-encode compatibility remains required.
The v4 specification makes contribution acceptance and transcript binding core invariants; v3 checks remain required.
The crypto-core boundary does not replace atomic filesystem publication.
A typed staging owner narrows cleanup drift; platform RAII and failure tests remain required.
V4 secret-owning types and provider capabilities make destruction evidence explicit; v3 dependency features remain required.
One v4 structural validator owns acceptance and is checked against independent vectors; the v3 validator remains required.
Checked v4 geometry is shared by reader and writer; v3 writer enforcement remains required.
The v4 parser contract is bounded, while each CLI and UI adapter still needs resource tests.

tradeoffs.assessment: Explicit version dispatch and a small typed core centralize suite, parser, transcript, and publication invariants; new design and model risk remain.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Require normative spec, pure model, production implementation, and independent vectors to agree on canonical and adversarial cases.

tradeoffs.assessment: AES-GCM provider performance, header overhead, version dispatch, and hybrid choices can change throughput and latency.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark identical file/pipe, signed/unsigned, recipient-set, and hardware workloads for v3 and v4 before changing defaults.

tradeoffs.assessment: Bounded chunks and parsers can preserve runtime limits, while parallel code and providers increase binary footprint; proof scratch is quota-bounded.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak RSS, binary size, temporary disk, proof scratch, retained evidence, and cleanup remainder.

tradeoffs.assessment: Version failures are contained and v3 remains recoverable, but carrying two readers creates maintenance risk.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise cross-version refusal, read recovery, opt-in disablement, stale evidence, and rollback with both fixture sets.

tradeoffs.assessment: The project must own two readers, suite inventory, evidence gates, resource quotas, and version-aware UI state.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run release and incident playbooks for proof refusal, v4 write disablement, and v3/v4 support diagnosis.

tradeoffs.assessment: New APIs, fixtures, documentation, and UI are required, but existing ciphertext is not forced through bulk migration.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Introduce read-only then opt-in stages, preserve all v3 fixtures, and complete rollback before any default change.

residualRisks: The v4 protocol and implementation can contain new composition defects.
The v3 compatibility reader remains security-sensitive.
Formal model-to-code correspondence remains an explicit review obligation.
Approved algorithms and local conformance vectors do not create CAVP or CMVP validation.
Platform, dependency, compiler, entropy, I/O, and side-channel behavior remain partly outside the pure formal core.

workPackages: Establish the versioned claim/evidence schema and vocabulary guard.
Build the storage-bounded proof runner and atomic evidence publisher.
Make the remediated v3 compatibility baseline reproducible.
Freeze the v4 threat model, suite, hybrid decision, grammar, and failure semantics.
Implement the isolated v4 checked core and exact version dispatcher.
Connect pure models, production code, independent vectors, and symbolic protocol claims.
Integrate truthful format/evidence state into CLI, Vault, and plugin.
Roll out read-only, opt-in, benchmark, recovery, and default-decision gates.
acceptanceCriteria: Every claim is revision-bound, scoped, and preserves its non-claims.
Proof runs remain under configured storage ceilings and fail atomically.
V3 compatibility and remediated invariants do not regress.
V3 and v4 are disjoint and requested v4 never falls back.
The v4 specification, model, independent vectors, and production code agree.
Rollback disables v4 writes while retaining v3 and created-v4 read access.
No artifact claims CAVP or CMVP validation without matching external certificate evidence.
migrationNotes: Start with evidence and read-only dispatch, then explicit opt-in writes.
Change defaults only after measured performance, resource, interoperability, recovery, and rollback gates pass.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Disable new v4 writes, retain the last known-good v4 reader for created data, preserve the v3 reader, and mark affected evidence revoked or superseded without relabeling formats.

options.title: Replace the current engine and migrate in place
options.summary: Collapse onto one candidate engine and require deployed ciphertext and integrations to migrate rather than carrying a long-lived v3 compatibility reader.

findingCoverage.rationale: A replacement may own publication safely, but migration introduces another plaintext publication path.
Replacing the crypto engine does not inherently redesign desktop collector lifecycle.
A replacement can use typed attestations, but migration and UI binding remain unspecified.
A replacement API may separate channels, but no implemented interface establishes that property.
Crypto replacement does not inherently fix process cancellation generations.
An honestly new version can prevent future encoding ambiguity, but in-place semantics under v3 would recreate the defect.
The replacement combiner and contributory checks are not yet specified.
Migration expands publication work and requires its own atomic no-clobber design.
Bulk migration expands temporary plaintext and ciphertext lifetime.
Replacement dependency and secret-owner behavior are not yet established.
A new parser can centralize validation but also creates a fresh differential risk during migration.
Replacement geometry is not yet modeled or implemented.
A replacement and migration inventory can each introduce new unbounded input paths.

tradeoffs.assessment: One steady-state core reduces duplicated ownership, but bulk decrypt/re-encrypt introduces a privileged plaintext and availability path.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Specify and test migration publication, provenance, interruption, resume, and dual verification before touching user data.

tradeoffs.assessment: Steady-state performance may improve or regress, while migration throughput and downtime dominate rollout.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark the replacement and a full dry-run migration against an inventory-shaped disposable corpus.

tradeoffs.assessment: The core can be bounded, but migration inventory, dual ciphertext retention, and recovery storage are unmeasured.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak RSS, old-plus-new ciphertext storage, temporary plaintext, proof scratch, and backup capacity.

tradeoffs.assessment: Interruption, missing identities, failed destination publication, and asymmetric rollback can make existing data unavailable.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise interruption and restoration at each migration transition while preserving the source container.

tradeoffs.assessment: Inventory, backup, identity availability, resume, recovery, and incident response become rollout-critical.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Complete operator playbooks and a disposable end-to-end recovery exercise before considering migration.

tradeoffs.assessment: Existing ciphertext and integrations must move, and code rollback cannot by itself read already-converted data.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove inventory completeness, preserve dual readers through rollback, and independently verify every converted artifact.

residualRisks: Bulk migration exposes more plaintext lifecycle and availability risk than an additive format.
Changing semantics under the v3 version line would create deliberate format ambiguity.
Code rollback is insufficient after data conversion without retained compatible readers.
A replacement core still requires external CAVP and CMVP processes for validation claims.

workPackages: Inventory deployed ciphertext and identity availability without reading user secrets.
Specify a distinct replacement format and migration state machine.
Build dual verification, backup, resume, rollback, and recovery tooling.
Migrate only after source-preserving dry runs and explicit operator approval.
acceptanceCriteria: Every source container remains intact until the replacement is independently verified.
Interrupted migration is resumable and rollback retains a compatible reader.
No replacement bytes use the v3 version line.
migrationNotes: Not selected under current compatibility and storage constraints.
Requires a separate data-inventory and recovery decision.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Retain both readers and original containers; code reversion alone is not a sufficient rollback after conversion.

opportunities.recommendation: Select the additive v4 candidate under current constraints, apply the v3 evidence discipline immediately, keep v4 opt-in until specification, proof, interoperability, resource, recovery, and rollback gates pass, and never describe the result as CAVP or CMVP validated without external certificate evidence.

openQuestions: Which current NIST-approved classical key-establishment method, or explicitly non-approved auxiliary contribution, should the v4 hybrid profile use?
Which exact approved key-wrap and KDF profiles fit the final v4 transcript and provider boundary?
What operator-configured free-space, scratch, retained-evidence, benchmark, and CI retention thresholds apply?
Which formal toolchain beyond Kani is supportable for protocol and model-to-code obligations?
What observed evidence should govern v4 opt-in, default selection, and long-term v3 writer support?
